paper_title: EditHero: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Part-Level 3D Editing and Vibe Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 3D editing methods are usually tested on a single edit, yet an asset is built through a long sequence of revisions, each of which must implement the requested change while leaving everything else unchanged. We introduce EditHero, to our knowledge the first benchmark for long-horizon, part-level 3D editing, with natural-language instructions and target images for both geometry and texture. A deterministic assembly engine produces the exact target after every edit, and every sequence is reviewed by hand. We use EditHero to compare 2 opposite approaches to 3D editing. Non-agentic methods operate top down, regenerating the object from a learned 3D representation and inferring what to keep. In contrast, LLM/VLM agents operate bottom up, editing through code that inspects the mesh and rewrites only the parts required by instructions. The non-agentic methods often miss the requested change and disturb regions that should stay fixed. Most LLMs follow instructions more closely, and all of them preserve the unedited parts better, but each of their edits takes minutes. We will release the engine and the edit sequences to support research on reliable iterative 3D editing.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: A 3D artist rarely makes one edit and stops. Assets in art and game production evolve through successive editing and revisions: each turn of modification changes part of the current asset while preserving earlier work. The same expectation underlies the recent concept of vibe modeling, in which users shape assets through an iterative natural-language conversation [184, 214, 36]. Yet textand image-guided 3D editing methods [98, 216, 199, 193] are typically evaluated on single edit from clean source. It remains unclear whether they can edit their own outputs repeatedly without losing earlier changes or degrading the asset. Evaluating this ability requires reference after every turn. Existing paired datasets [199, 216, 193] only provide isolated edits. Their targets come from either learned editing models or changes to poses and semantic parts. Neither design can tell us whether method preserves earlier changes across sequence of instructions. We introduce EditHero, benchmark of part-level edit chains with exact ground truth (Figure 2). The benchmark is built with the help of data engine, which assembles library parts onto segmented host objects with 4 operations (add, remove, replace and retexture) and records every operation in JSON file. Each entry is single atomic operation, so replaying the file with the part library rebuilds the exact state after any turn. After human review, EditHero contains 457 chains and 2755 edits across 252 objects, with up to 30 turns per chain (Section 3). We test 2 families of methods on this long-horizon 3D editing task, and they approach an edit in opposite ways. Non-agentic methods work top down. They regenerate the edited object from learned 3D representation, such as the latents of diffusion model, so every turn changes every corner of the asset, more or less. In contrast, LLM/VLM agents work bottom up. An LLM or VLM inspects the current mesh and writes code that changes only the named part. This keeps everything else untouched by construction and forces every new part to be built from primitives. We compare 4 non-agentic methods [193, 216, 199, 98] with 6 LLM/VLM agents under self-rollout protocol (Section 4), in which every edit starts from the methods own previous output. We also design 2 metrics to measure the differences between these methods, including instruction following (IF) inside the edit region and content consistency (CC) outside it. The results indicate that agentic methods have superior editing ability. The non-agentic methods often miss the requested change as early as the first turn, and errors accumulate along chain. The colors of their results also shift away from the target. The agents behave differently. Most agents follow instructions more closely than non-agentic methods, and all agents keep the untouched parts better. However, the agents speed is not so satisfying, as single edit takes minutes rather than seconds (Sections 5 and 5.4). Our contributions are: Generation engine. We construct data synthesis engine that produces part-level edit chains with an exact target after every turn. Benchmark. We propose EditHero, human-reviewed benchmark for long-horizon part-level 3D editing. Evaluation framework. We evaluate 4 non-agentic methods and 6 LLM/VLM agents under self-rollout, with region-specific measures of instruction following and preservation.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: 3D editing. 3D editing has followed the available generative models. Early methods optimized NeRF or Gaussian splat under 2D diffusion prior [61, 28, 22], and later ones edit rendered views or an image and then reconstruct the object [7, 66]. Part-level and sketch-based methods let user refine an object step by step [41, 157, 94, 97]. Native 3D generators such as TRELLIS [200] made it possible to edit 3D latent directly. Methods trained on paired edits feed the source latent to the generator through an added branch, much as ControlNet [234] conditions an image model. PartFlow [193] adds source-control branch, and 3DEditFormer [199] uses dual-guidance attention. Training-free methods reuse pretrained generator instead. VoxHammer [98] inverts the source and reuses its cached latents and attention features in the 2 preserved region, and Nano3D [216] follows the difference between the source-conditioned and targetconditioned flows, using the FlowEdit formulation [89]. We evaluate PartFlow, 3DEditFormer, VoxHammer and Nano3D as representatives. Each was proposed and evaluated for one edit at time, and each uses generative latents to synthesize edited content. EditHero instead asks them to keep editing their own output, as an artist would, and measures what regeneration does to the parts not required by any instruction. Appendix describes these methods in more detail and lists the others. 3D editing benchmarks. Most textand image-guided 3D editing benchmarks score one instruction at time. Some pair source asset with target asset, obtained through image-guided generation [199, 216, 126] or pose and part changes [199, 193, 145]. Others have no target asset and score region preservation and alignment to an edited image instead [98, 251, 53, 135], and scene-level benchmarks follow the same pattern [143, 115, 253]. The closest multi-step settings are agent benchmarks such as BlenderGym [58] and 3DCodeBench [52], which let an agent iterate toward one fixed goal. EZBlender [178] instead bundles several edits into one prompt. To our knowledge, EditHero is the first benchmark to evaluate different natural-language part edits in sequence on one asset, with an exact 3D reference after every turn (Appendix Table 4). LLM/VLM agents for 3D generation and editing. LLM agents can modify 3D assets through code. They write programs or call tools to build scenes [166, 208] and edit Blender scenes from renders [69, 121]. Related systems generate objects and CAD programs [35, 83, 155]. Recent systems treat the program itself as the asset and revise it under visual feedback [109, 137, 184], aiming to keep edits local and preserve the rest of the state. Our data engine also records edits as operations that can be replayed to reconstruct each state. We evaluate such agents on the mesh, turn by turn and with the same metrics as the non-agentic methods (Section 5.4).

sections.title: 3 Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Task. We hope to do multi-turn editing starting from textured, part-segmented host object S0 with text or image conditions. We define 4 operations, add, remove, replace and retexture. Each turn specifies one operation on part through text instruction and fixed-view render of the target state. An add attaches part to free contact face, and remove deletes named part, which may consist of several pieces. replace swaps named part for another at the same location, while retexture changes how part looks without touching its geometry. All other parts should remain unchanged. After each turn, the method returns 3D object that becomes its input at the next turn. Text instructions may refer to earlier edits. For example, part added at one turn can be removed few turns later, so method may want to keep track of what it has already built. Exact ground truth by construction. Evaluating chain requires reliable target at every turn. Some existing paired datasets obtain their targets from image-guided generative pipelines [199, 216], and such target can itself contain changes nobody asked for. We instead assemble each target from parts, much as CLEVR and Kubric generate their scenes programmatically [79, 57]. For an addition or replacement, the engine retrieves caption-matched parts from library built from PartVerse-XL [40], Objaverse-XL [38] and HY3D-Bench [173]. It then screens the candidates with vision-language model (VLM) and tests their placement for contact, scale, connectivity, and interpenetration. Removal deletes the part occupying named slot. For retexture, the engine renders the slot and restyles the render with an image editing model (Qwen-Image-Edit [194]). The texturing module of TRELLIS.2 [201] then textures the unchanged slot geometry from the restyled image. Each chain is stored as JSON file that logs every accepted operation with its library part, pose and texture. Together with the part library, the log rebuilds any state Sk exactly and records what changed at each turn. Human review. Reviewers inspect renders of every turn for incorrect parts, orientation, placement, scale, ambiguous instructions, and broken dependencies. They correct flagged cases by editing the logged operations and rebuilding the affected turns. They also rewrite instructions drafted from part captions to describe the intended part, position, and orientation clearly. sections.title: 4 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: Setting. We evaluate the editing methods under self-rollout, in which turn takes the methods own output from turn 1 as input. At each turn method receives its current state, the instruction and the target render, and VoxHammer also receives ground-truth edit mask. Ground-truth states are used only for scoring. All states of chain share one coordinate frame and 4 fixed camera views, 1 conditioning view and 3 held-out views. Image metrics are averaged over the 4 views, and Appendix reports the conditioning view and the held-out views separately. Scores are averaged over the turns method completes. Appendix provides details. Design of metrics. Previous 3D editing evaluations follow 2 designs. When target asset exists, they compare the edited object with it as whole, using Chamfer distance, normal consistency, F-score and image similarity of the renders [199, 193, 126, 145]. Without target asset, they measure how well the unedited region keeps the source object and judge the edit by its similarity to an edited image or to the text [98, 216, 251, 53, 135, 143]. Both designs score single edit applied to clean source object. sections.title: 5.1 Setup
sections.content: We evaluate 4 non-agentic 3D methods, PartFlow [193], Nano3D [216], 3DEditFormer [199] and VoxHammer [98], with their released code, weights and sampling settings. Each of these 4 methods runs under self-rollout on all 457 chains (2755 turns) and receives, at each turn, its own previous output, the instruction and the target render in the fixed view of the chain. VoxHammer also receives the ground-truth edit mask. Nano3D has no material mode, so its material turns run in its replace mode. We also run the no-op and regeneration baselines of Section 4. Appendix describes the method settings and execution coverage.

sections.title: 5.4 Comparison with LLM/VLM agents
sections.content: An LLM agent inspects the current mesh, writes code to add, remove, replace or retexture parts, and checks rendered views before it commits an edit. We evaluate 6 models: GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Sol 6, Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5. Each chain is assigned to an independent agent using the same editing prompt. New parts must be built through code; external part libraries and generative 3D or image models are not allowed. Appendix gives the setup. We compare these agents with the 4 non-agentic methods and both baselines on shared comparison subset of 55 chains (416 turns). We selected chains with clearly visible edits that resemble an artists revisions, covering all 6 families and range of operation combinations. The editing methods use self-rollout. Table 3 reports the comparison, and Appendix shows additional examples. LLMs preserve more and usually follow instructions better. All 6 LLMs keep the rest of the object better than any non-agentic method (CCprev 0.950.98 against at most 0.90). All except GLM 5.3 Flash also follow instructions better (IF up to 0.62 for Opus 5.5, against at most 0.36). sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: EditHero tests whether 3D editing method can perform successive edits on an asset over many turns. Because its chains are assembled from parts, the correct state after every turn is known exactly, so we can score the requested change and the rest of the object separately. The non-agentic methods, which regenerate the whole object at every turn, often miss the edit from the first turn and let the unedited parts drift as the chain grows. On whole-object F-score, LPIPS and PSNR they even fall behind simply returning the input. LLM agents, which change only the parts required by instructions, keep the remainder of the asset intact, and most of them also follow instructions more closely. It seems that the agentic approach is naturally suited to editing. However, building new geometry from code remains hard, and an edit that takes minutes is still too slow for interactive work. It remains an open question whether we can find proper combination of agentic and conventional methods that is both fast and accurate. We will release the data synthesis engine and the edit chains for further 3D editing research.

sections.title: A Extended related work
sections.content: 3D generation. An influential line of text-to-3D generation optimizes 3D representation against 2D diffusion prior [144, 108, 186], with related approaches using multi-view diffusion [117, 160, 120] and feed-forward reconstruction [65, 205]. Current systems train diffusion or flow model directly on native 3D latent, which may be vector set [228, 246, 232, 103, 247, 174, 101] or triplane [197], or sparse or structured voxel grid [200, 201, 104, 213]. All 4 non-agentic methods we evaluate build on the structured latent of TRELLIS [200]. separate line generates low-polygon, artist-style meshes autoregressively, one face or one token at time [133, 162, 26, 30, 29, 191, 187, 169, 192, 241, 111, 185, 165, 85, 60] or by flow matching in mesh latent space [102, 176]. These methods target compact mesh structure rather than instructionguided changes to an existing asset. TAR3D [236] autoregressively predicts quantized triplane tokens, while SeamFlow [245] predicts cuts for UV unwrapping on an existing mesh. Part-aware modeling includes segmentation [210, 116, 122], generative decomposition and completion [211, 233, 207, 100], and generation of objects as sets of parts [24, 110, 212, 170, 25, 224, 254, 106]. Assembler [242] places input parts into complete object, while SIMART and PWM-ArtGen address articulated assets [229, 248]. Texture synthesis is line of work of its own [153, 18, 226, 220, 158], including PBR material generation [163, 71, 63, 31, 47, 221, 203]. EditHero applies retexturing to one part while requiring the rest of the object to remain unchanged. CMD [99] supports progressive generation and local editing by conditioning on known parts. Its progressive examples illustrate construction, whereas EditHero supplies benchmark of different instructions and exact reference states along each chain. EditHero uses the parts of an object both as the unit of editing and to build the exact ground truth. Additional 3D editing methods. The methods we evaluate come from the 2 main families built on native 3D latents. Trained methods learn from paired edits. Much as ControlNet [234] conditions an image model, they feed the source latent to the generator through an added control branch. PartFlow [193] does this with source-control branch, and 3DEditFormer [199] does it with dual-guidance attention [see also 14, 53, 222]. Training-free methods reuse pretrained generators without edit-specific training. Inversionbased methods such as VoxHammer [98] invert the source along the sampling trajectory and reuse its cached latents and attention keys and values in the preserved region. Inversion-free methods follow the difference between the source-conditioned and target-conditioned flows. Nano3D [216] does this with the FlowEdit formulation [89], and related variants follow the same idea [251, 135, 67]. Single-view regeneration from the target render, which we report as reference, is the limiting case of regenerating the object from an edited image. Further approaches are discussed below. Early editing methods modify neural field or Gaussian splat with 2D diffusion prior [61, 156, 256, 28, 179, 82, 257, 195, 22], and some of them take sketches [130, 114] or drag handles [148] as conditions instead of text. Recent methods also use mesh reconstruction or native 3D latents [23, 19, 146, 84, 7, 141, 251, 53, 66, 32, 21, 222, 215, 1, 142]. Other systems edit Gaussian scenes or scene atlases [161, 46]. Object insertion in 3D scenes and 3D object inpainting are also studied separately [96, 48]. Part-level and interactive methods let user act on one part at time [41, 42, 177, 157, 164], and sketch-based systems have supported iterative refinement since Teddy [77, 134, 94, 95, 59, 10, 249, 6, 97, 92, 93, 238]. Sketch2CAD [94] and MeshPad [97] support sequential sketch-based modeling. Their evaluations focus on sketch interpretation and interactive modeling, whereas EditHero evaluates sequence of natural-language part edits against exact 3D references. 2D image editing and its evaluation. Instruction-based image editing developed from inversion, personalization and attention control [128, 5, 64, 51, 154, 132, 34, 81, 175, 15, 234, 11] to models trained on edit pairs [13, 159, 55, 50, 240, 75, 223, 190, 147] and to unified generators that edit in context [202, 239, 118, 90, 194, 39]. Geometry-aware image editing uses 3D cues for spatial transformations or object removal [9, 62, 255], and BlenderFusion [20] combines 3D scene manipulation with generative image compositing. Before diffusion, iterative editing was studied as human-in-the-loop optimization, in which Bayesian optimization searches the parameters of an image or an animation under human preference feedback [12, 56, 87, 88]. Recent work applies the same idea to generative image search or adapter merging [151, 112]. These systems study iterative improvement under human feedback. Benchmarks for image editing [182, 231, 8, 124, 218, 243, 198, 54] 23 established that did it edit and did it leave the rest alone must be scored separately, and that similarity to the source mixes up the requested change with drift. Multi-turn image evaluations use reference images or VLM judge [231, 252, 125, 70, 227, 209, 27]. DiffSeg30k [33] instead uses multi-turn edits to benchmark localized detection of generated content. MagicBrush provides intermediate target images reviewed by human annotators [231]. EditHero instead supplies complete 3D reference states that can be rebuilt deterministically, with the edited parts known at every turn. Multi-turn methods respond with memory of earlier turns or reinforcement learning over the sequence [230, 204, 219]. Repeated image replication can accumulate artifacts that no-reference quality metrics fail to capture [171]. Related work studies different sources of accumulated error: repeated training on synthetic outputs [2, 237] and exposure bias within diffusion sampling [136]. We study successive 3D edits at inference time, where holes, loose pieces and displacement can be computed directly. Additional LLM/VLM and agentic methods. LLMs can build 3D content by writing procedural code or calling tools. They do this for scenes and layouts [166, 36, 68, 208, 49, 168] and for editing an existing scene in Blender from renders [69, 121, 178, 140]. Related code-based systems generate objects and CAD programs [225, 80, 35, 83, 155, 3, 127, 91]. Recent systems treat the program as the asset itself, with an agent that plans, writes and revises procedural code under visual feedback [109, 181, 138, 113, 137, 4]. EmbodiedGen V2 [184] describes this as vibe coding of 3D worlds through dialogue of instructions, aiming to make local edits while preserving the rest of the state. EditHero measures this workflow. Agentic pipelines exist for images as well [188, 119, 17, 206, 123, 217, 244, 105, 196, 74, 72]. Related VLM-guided editing models and unified generators use learned multimodal reasoning [73, 45, 107]. Benchmarks for these agents [58, 52] score the final state against one goal. Ground truth by construction. Part-annotated collections [16, 131, 180, 40] and procedural asset generators [250, 150] provide objects and parts for assembly. EditHero builds its chains with program, like synthetic benchmarks whose targets are produced by program [79, 57, 37] and unlike annotated datasets. The assembly engine that produces each state is deterministic, and rebuilding turn from its logged operations reproduces the state exactly. The engine does not guarantee quality, so every chain went through manual review (Appendix B). Comparison with existing benchmarks. 3DEditVerse [199] combines pose changes with image-guided appearance edits, while Nano3D-Edit-100k [216] uses native 3D editing method guided by edited images. Uni3DEdit-Bench [193] uses semantic-part transformations, and Delta3D [145] removes parts from CAD assemblies. Steer3D's EDIT3D-BENCH [126] and the editing subset of 3D-Alpaca [214] reconstruct edited images into target assets. Edit3D-Bench [98], Eval3DEdit [251], BenchUp [53] and EditFlow-Bench [135] have no target asset, so they score region preservation and alignment to an edited image instead. Scene-level benchmarks follow the same pattern [143, 115, 253]. Each sample specifies single editing goal, represented by an asset or an edited image. BlenderGym [58] and 3DCodeBench [52] let an agent iterate toward one fixed goal, and EZBlender [178] bundles several edits into one prompt. Table 4 places EditHero next to these benchmarks. The table compares target construction, instruction sequences, intermediate references and evaluation on each methods own outputs.

sections.title: B Benchmark construction details
sections.content: Why assemble the targets? Assembling target needs suitable part and plausible placement. The part has to make sense on the object (for example, hat on head or barrel on porch) and be attached where person would attach it. Accepted placements must also satisfy explicit geometric constraints and stay reproducible after repair. We therefore combine deterministic placement checks with manual review of every chain. Hosts and slots. Our part library mainly contains PartVerse-XL [40], whose objects come from ObjaverseXL [38]. We also use very few parts from HY3D-Bench [173]. They come without texture, so we texture them with the same pipeline as the retexture turns. For retrieval, we generate part descriptions with 24 Table 4 EditHero compared with existing editing benchmarks. Each chain starts from textured, part-segmented object, which we call the host. Its parts are grouped into small number of slots. slot is sub-assembly, such as head, an arm or porch canopy, that an instruction can name and that is large enough to see in render. Slots are proposed automatically from the part contact graph and the part captions, and then accepted, merged or renamed by reviewer looking at highlighted renders. Reviewers also correct the proposed slot names so they describe the grouped parts clearly. Operations. Add places new part from the library on free face of an existing part, remove deletes the part or part group occupying named slot, replace swaps the part in slot for retrieved one on the same contact face, and retexture repaints slot and leaves its geometry exactly as it was. The new texture comes from render of the slot restyled by Qwen-Image-Edit [194] and is applied to the unchanged slot geometry by the texturing module of TRELLIS.2 [201]. Before support part is replaced, its attachments are removed in separate turns, and they are reattached in separate turns as well. Each step thus stays an explicit operation on named part or part group. Instructions use natural-language part descriptions and never contain internal slot identifiers or library metadata. Placement. Placement is deterministic, as in procedural datasets whose labels come from the generating program [79, 57, 150]. For replacement or an add-on part, the engine retrieves candidates by the similarity of their caption embeddings to the requested part [183, 152]. It computes an initial pose from the hosts contact face (a planar, axial or point mate, depending on the slot), scales the part so that its mount matches the face (between 0.75 and 2 times its original size) and snaps it into contact. Automatic candidate screening then applies 4 checks. contact frame must exist, the remaining gap must be below 0.01 of the object diagonal, the object must stay one connected piece under that tolerance, and the interpenetration fraction must stay below 0.02. The automatic search rejects candidates that fail check and tries the next one. Human review then assesses whether the assembly is visually appropriate, including intentional overlaps or disconnected components in stylized hosts. Chain recipe. Each chain is stored as JSON file that names the host and has one entry per turn. An entry gives the slot, the library part for an addition or replacement, the accepted pose and, for retexture, the 25 generated texture. Slots that turn does not name stay as they were. With the part library, the file rebuilds any state Sk = ok( o1(S0)) on its own, without repeating retrieval or texture generation. repair edits the entry of one turn, and that turn and the later ones are rebuilt and checked again. Human review and repair. Every turn was rendered from several views before and after the edit and inspected. Reviewers flagged wrong part semantics (a foot placed as hand), wrong orientation or mounting, implausible scale, instructions that gave away the source or were ambiguous, and dependency errors (an attachment silently carried along when its parent was replaced). Reviewers corrected poses in the operation log, saved revised geometry or materials as separate assets when needed, and rebuilt the affected turns. Original source assets were retained. Turns that could not be fixed were cut, and the rest of the chain was rebuilt from that point. Families. Chains are grouped by the operations they contain. Family holds mostly additions. Families and contain only removals and replacements, respectively. Family contains only material edits. Family mixes geometry operations, and family mixes geometry and material operations. The benchmark contains 141 A, 72 M, 45 R, 54 P, 85 and 60 chains. Taking the 6 families together, we try to keep the share of each operation stable and even from turn to turn. sections.title: C Evaluation protocol details
sections.content: Self-rollout. We give each method the initial mesh and, at turn k, the instruction together with the conditions it needs, such as target image or mask. Its input at turn is its own output at turn 1. The main evaluation never resets the state to the ground truth, and Appendix reports separate diagnostic that does. If method fails turn, for example with an empty or unloadable output, the rest of that chain is blocked and the chain counts as failure. This rule is the same for the non-agentic methods and the LLM/VLM agents, and we never restart from the ground truth to rescue chain. Infrastructure faults are handled separately (Appendix F). Conditioning. Every method receives the same target image at given turn, rendered with the chains fixed conditioning camera, and VoxHammer also receives an edit mask. The target image shows what the object should look like after the edit. shared coordinate frame and fixed views. We measure all states of chain, ground truth and outputs alike, in one frame normalized by the bounding box of all its ground-truth states. We render them with one camera rig fitted to the bounding sphere of those states. The rig has 4 views 90 apart at one elevation, fixed focal length and fixed lighting. If we re-centered every turn or every part, part that moved would look as if it had stayed in place, and new camera at every turn would make image metrics incomparable across turns. One default direction for all chains, however, can hide the edited part, since small addition on the far side of the object barely shows in the conditioning view. We therefore choose the direction per chain. For every turn, the edited region is the set of part nodes whose geometry or material differs between the previous and the current ground-truth state. We fix for the chain the direction that makes its worst turn most visible (Appendix E). To estimate visibility, we cast rays from surface samples of that region toward each candidate direction against the full state. Because the rig is fitted to all states of the chain, its framing reflects how large the object will become. No method receives the rig as geometry, and every method still sees the object in its own frame, fixed at the initial state. Why these definitions. The definitions follow the design of Section 4, and Figure 6 shows examples of the problems they avoid. Score the edit and the rest separately. turn changes only small part of an object. On the whole object, returning the initial object can therefore score higher than doing the requested edit on state that has already drifted (Figure 6b). We therefore split every metric into Ek, Uk and the whole object. We take the regions from the named parts rather than from voxel or pixel differences, because retexture leaves the ground-truth geometry unchanged even when method changes it (Figure 6d). Using the named parts in both the old and the new state covers all 4 operations with one definition. The one-cell dilation absorbs part that lands one cell off, so small misplacement lowers IF but is not counted second time as damage in CC. Measure each turn against the methods own previous output. Suppose chain removes hat at turn 2 and adds it back at turn 5. If we took the required addition from the ground truth, that is, the voxels present at turn 5 and absent at turn 4, the no-op output would already contain the hat and get full credit, although it never did anything. We instead take the required addition from the methods own previous output. The no-op output then needs nothing and gets no credit, and method that did remove the hat gets credit only when it puts the hat back. For the same reason, part lost at an earlier turn does not count as successful removal now (Figure 6a). IF also catches replacement that only deletes the old part. Its IF is close to 0 because the new part is missing, while its F-score to the target is within 0.02 of the no-op baseline (Figure 6c). CCprev uses the same anchor and asks whether this turn disturbed what it should keep. CC0 compares with the initial object and shows how far the untouched content has drifted over the whole chain. sections.title: E Camera search
sections.content: For each chain and each candidate camera direction, we sample points on the edited region of every turn and cast rays toward the camera against the full state. The visible projected area, weighted by the cosine to the view direction and corrected for depth, is divided by the frame area at the object center. The chosen direction is the one whose worst turn is most visible, with small preference for the default direction. The estimate correlates with the measured pixel change of the rendered views at Spearman ρ = 0.95.

sections.content: We evaluate PartFlow [193], Nano3D [216], 3DEditFormer [199], and VoxHammer [98] with their released code and weights. Each method is wrapped in an adapter that only supplies inputs and records outputs. The sampling code, seeds and hyperparameters are the authors own. PartFlow, Nano3D and 3DEditFormer take the current state and the target render. VoxHammer also takes the ground-truth edit mask. Nano3Ds official interface has add, remove and replace modes but no material mode. With the official routing, Nano3D rejects material instruction and the rest of the chain is blocked, which would happen on all 132 chains that contain one. We therefore route every material instruction to the replace mode. The adapter passes the unchanged instruction text and the target render exactly as for replace turn, and the output is scored like any other turn. The Nano3D rows use this routing on those 132 chains and the official routing on the other chains. All methods are scored with the same fixed-camera protocol of Section 4. The meshes of the 4 methods, exported through TRELLIS, carry no metallic value and would render as dark metal, so we render them as non-metallic. The agents outputs of Section 5.4 set their own materials and are rendered as exported. The TRELLIS regeneration baseline runs the released TRELLIS-image-large pipeline [200] on the target render of every turn, in the same fixed view that the non-agentic methods receive. sections.content: Geometry metrics do not register material edits, so we measure them in images. For every retexture turn we take the pixels where the ground-truth render changes. Nano3D, whose material turns run in the replace mode, changes the region by 0.31 times the ground-truth image change, and its distance to the target is close to that of its own unedited previous output.
